name: Eritrea
card_headline: Eritrea cut ties with Ethiopia on 1 October as each accuses the other of aggression in Tigray, and the US let its sanctions lapse in September.
card_summary: Eritrea severed diplomatic ties with Ethiopia on 1 October. Ethiopia told the UN Security Council that Eritrean troops advanced up to 60 km into Tigray, which Asmara rejects while accusing Addis Ababa of aiming at the port of Assab. [1][2] Washington let sanctions on Eritrea's ruling party and military expire in September. [3] At home, national service is indefinite and independent media are banned. [4]
card_local: Eritrea has no independent domestic press, so this lens rests on outlets in Addis Ababa and Nairobi. The Reporter relays the Information Ministry's statements, and the Nation reports Eritrea's appeal to the UN Security Council. [5][6]
card_international: AFP, Reuters and AP report the diplomatic break, Ethiopia's letter to the Security Council and the sanctions decision, and say the troop claims could not be independently verified. [2][7][3]
card_scholar: Crisis Group (February) named Assab as the most likely objective of any limited Ethiopian campaign, and the UN Special Rapporteur (May) urged both sides to halt military build-ups. [8][9]
context_md: Eritrea became independent from Ethiopia in 1993, and President Isaias Afwerki has ruled since then with no national election. [4] The two countries fought a border war from 1998 to 2000, made peace in 2018 and fought on the same side against Tigrayan forces in the 2020 to 2022 war. [2][10] Eritrea was not a party to the 2022 Pretoria agreement that ended that war, and relations soured soon afterwards. [2] Independent media have been banned since September 2001, and the government controls domestic media. [4] National service should legally last 18 months but has been extended indefinitely since a 1998 state of emergency. [4] Ethiopia has been landlocked since Eritrea's independence, and Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed says it has a right to sea access, which Eritrea reads as a threat to Assab. [2]

sections.title: Ties are cut and both capitals say the other started it
sections.body_md:
Ethiopia announced it would close its embassy in Asmara and expel 10 Eritrean diplomats. Eritrea answered on 1 October by severing diplomatic ties, and said Ethiopia hosts, trains and arms Eritrean opposition groups. Ethiopia cited Eritrea's "direct and indirect acts of hostility". [1]

On 8 October Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos wrote to the UN Security Council accusing Eritrea of an "all-out invasion" and saying Eritrean troops had advanced up to 60 km into Tigray. [2] AP reports that the letter invokes Article 51 of the UN Charter but does not say what measures Ethiopia is taking, which areas are occupied or what evidence supports the claim. AP could not verify it. [7] Eritrea's Information Minister, Yemane Gebremeskel, called the conflict an unprovoked war of aggression and said Abiy's October 2023 remarks on sea access were a declaration of war. [11] Foreign Minister Osman Saleh wrote to the Council invoking Chapter VII and asking it to act against Addis Ababa. [6]

Accounts differ on whether Asmara denies the crossings. Reuters reported that Yemane did not deny that troops had crossed and called Ethiopia's self-defense account a "fallacious narrative". [12] AP says he neither confirmed nor denied it. [7] The Nation and the Critical Threats Project, a US research group, both say Eritrea denies its troops are in Ethiopia. [6][13]

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio spoke to Abiy on 14 October and urged dialogue under the 2018 peace deal. [14]

The denial is not new. In March 2025 Yemane said Eritrean troops were deployed within Eritrea's own territory and that Eritrea had no interest in undermining the Pretoria agreement. [15] A further undated Garowe Online report has him rejecting a former Ethiopian president's claims that Eritrea drives conflict in Ethiopia and denying a continued military presence in border areas. [16]

lenses.local: The Nation reports Ethiopian army forces had reached Zalambessa, on the Ethiopian side of the border, according to six sources, and that it was unclear whether Eritrean troops or rebels remained there. [6]
lenses.international: AFP, AP and Reuters carry both governments' claims. Reuters witnesses saw dozens of Eritrean soldiers in Adigrat, and none of the wires could verify the 60 km advance. [12][2][7]
lenses.scholar: Hossamaldeen Ibrahim of the Bloomsbury Intelligence and Security Institute says severed ties removed the main crisis-management channel, and Matthias Rompel of Giessen University says Eritrean involvement is hard to verify independently. [10]

sections.title: The front in November: clashes near Rama and Badme, and a mobilisation report at Sawa that is unconfirmed
sections.body_md:
The most recent tracking comes from the Critical Threats Project. Its 17 November brief says federal and TPLF forces have clashed repeatedly around Rama, near the Ethiopia-Eritrea border, since 7 November. It says ACLED reported that Eritrean forces regained control of Badme by 15 November after fighting that began on 9 November with artillery and drone strikes, while other trackers said on 12 and 13 November that Eritrea no longer held it. A pro-Fano account claimed Eritrean forces were involved in clashes in Irob, northeast of Adigrat, and the brief could not confirm that. On 14 November X trackers reported a widespread Eritrean mobilisation at Sawa. The brief saw more satellite activity there from 14 to 16 November but could not confirm what it involved. [13]

October followed a similar pattern. Reuters witnesses saw dozens of Eritrean soldiers in trucks in Adigrat on 7 October. [12] ACLED reported Eritrean troops crossing near Zalambessa and coming under drone attack, which it attributed to Ethiopia's military. [7] By 15 October ACLED reported Ethiopian tanks and heavy weapons moving toward the Eritrean border and Eritrean troops withdrawing across it. A pro-government militia spokesman said Eritrean forces took significant casualties, which Yemane rejected and no one has verified. [17]

Human Rights Watch said it had received reports of civilians killed and injured by shelling in southern Tigray and that shelling had forced some health facilities to close. AP gives no total and does not say who fired. [14] Ethiopia's army chief, Birhanu Jula, visited Mekelle on 13 November and accused the TPLF of trying to separate Tigray from Ethiopia with Eritrean help. He also accused Egypt of supplying the rebels. [13]

lenses.local: The Nation noted that the Zalambessa picture was unclear in mid-October, with a pro-government militia spokesman not confirming that the army controlled the town. [6]
lenses.international: AFP, Anadolu and AP report the same incidents and flag each casualty and territorial claim as unverified. [17][14]
lenses.scholar: Critical Threats and ACLED are the main trackers, and Critical Threats marks each claim it could not confirm. [13]

sections.title: Assab: why Asmara reads Ethiopia's sea-access demand as a war aim
sections.body_md:
Crisis Group's February briefing says Abiy's stated goal of regaining sea access is viewed in Asmara as a possible threat, and that Assab, Eritrea's southern Red Sea port, is the most likely objective of any limited Ethiopian campaign. It adds that a January 2024 deal with Somaliland, which would have given Ethiopia a naval base, effectively collapsed after Turkiye brokered the Ankara Declaration in late 2024, which shifted attention back to Assab. [8] Chatham House (28 November 2025) says Eritrea calls the issue a redline and that the rhetoric of defending sovereignty is uniting Eritreans behind their leadership. [18]

Abiy told parliament in early November 2025 that sea access is an irreversible national interest, that Ethiopia would pursue it by peaceful means and that it does not intend to go to war with Eritrea. Eritrea's Information Minister replied that Ethiopia was pursuing "belligerent, reckless and unlawful policies". [5] In October 2026 Yemane also said Ethiopia had cited Israel's annexation of the Golan Heights as a precedent for its ambitions on Assab. That is Eritrea's claim, and AFP does not confirm it. [11]

Horn Review, an Addis Ababa outlet, says the Assab-Bure axis lies near the Djibouti-Semera corridor, which it says carries over 90 percent of Ethiopia's trade. It reports intelligence-source claims from 25 September of Eritrean brigades moving from the Assab front toward Berahle and Dalul in Afar, and notes that no independent source confirms an advance. [19] Ethiopia's Afar regional administrator said Eritrean troops were fighting in the area, which Reuters could not confirm. [12]

lenses.local: The Reporter in Addis Ababa carried Abiy's parliamentary line and Asmara's reply side by side. [5]
lenses.international: AFP carries Yemane's Golan precedent claim and his charge that Ethiopia has been at war with Eritrea since 2023. [11]
lenses.scholar: Crisis Group and Chatham House both treat Assab as the focal point and urge preventive diplomacy and pressure on Ethiopia not to move on it. [8][18]

sections.title: Washington let its Eritrea sanctions lapse in September, with no stated link to Ethiopia
sections.body_md:
US sanctions on Eritrea's ruling party and military lapsed on 18 September. [19] They had been imposed in November 2021 over abuses in the Tigray war. A Treasury notice said the national emergency under which they were renewed each year had expired, and the State Department said President Trump chose not to renew it. [3] The State Department said the step was taken to advance US regional interests, and that the parties' implementation of the Tigray peace deal had been uneven. Yemane welcomed it and said the sanctions had caused major damage. [3]

Semafor says no official reason was given. It points to its April report of Egypt-brokered talks between Isaias and a senior Africa adviser to Trump, and to a May Reuters report that the US planned to lift the sanctions. [20] Al Jazeera ties the decision to Eritrea's Red Sea position amid Houthi pressure on shipping through the Bab al-Mandeb. [3] On 5 August the US adviser Massad Boulos denied that Washington backs an anti-Ethiopia bloc, saying no such arrangement is under discussion. [21]

Casualty figures for the Tigray war itself vary by source. Al Jazeera says at least 600,000 people were killed, and Semafor says more than 100,000. [3][20]

lenses.local: The Reporter carried Boulos's August denial of an anti-Ethiopia bloc. No Eritrea-based outlet reported on the lapse in anything this draft could read. [21]
lenses.international: AFP, AP and Reuters report the lapse, and Semafor reports that no official reason was given. [3][20]
lenses.scholar: Horn Review notes the lapse in its October brief on Ethiopia's northern crisis and dates it to 18 September. [19]

sections.title: Egypt, Sudan and the Gulf: Eritrea's alliances and its second exit from IGAD
sections.body_md:
Eritrea announced on 12 December 2025 that it was leaving the Intergovernmental Authority on Development, saying the bloc had drifted from its founding principles. IGAD said it regretted the decision and noted that Eritrea had not taken part in its activities. [22] The UN Secretary-General's office urged Eritrea and Ethiopia to recommit to the 2000 Algiers Agreement. [23] Reports give different years for the first exit, 2003 in one account and 2007 in another. [23][22]

The Reporter says officials from Egypt, Eritrea and Somalia met in Cairo with a senior US envoy on 19 July 2026, and that Egypt and Eritrea then issued a joint declaration rejecting security arrangements imposed by non-littoral parties in the Red Sea. It also says Sudan's army chief, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, visited Asmara before the latest clashes. [21] Isaias made a five-day visit to Egypt in November 2025, and Asmara called speculation about it a "hysterical commotion". [5]

Horn Review researcher Tsega'ab Amare argues that Egypt and Eritrea both back Sudan's army, creating pressure on Ethiopia, and relays a claim by an eastern Sudan alliance that army-aligned militias were trained in Eritrea. The piece offers no independent evidence for that claim. [24] Ethiopia accuses Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt of backing the opposition alliance, and all three deny it. [12] A Saudi-led maritime coalition has 14 founding members and Eritrea is not among them. [21]

lenses.local: Ethiopian outlets, The Reporter and Horn Review among them, frame Egypt and Eritrea as aligned against Ethiopia, and the Reporter's own account of the Cairo meeting is presented as reported. [21][24]
lenses.international: Africanews and Yahoo carry Eritrea's exit from IGAD and the UN's call to recommit to the Algiers Agreement. [22][23]
lenses.scholar: Horn Review's analysis of Egypt, Eritrea and eastern Sudan is an opinion piece and rests on second-hand claims. [24]

sections.title: A command economy with no published budget, a pegged currency and one mine
sections.body_md:
The Bertelsmann Transformation Index 2026, which covers February 2023 to January 2025, describes a command economy in which the ruling party and the military dominate through state enterprises and the Hdri Trust Fund, with no state budget published since independence. [25] It says the World Bank has released no growth figures since 2011 and the IMF published no 2024 inflation rate, so this draft carries no current GDP figure. [25]

External debt was $725.9 million in 2023, and the African Development Bank put debt at 164 percent of GDP in 2022. The nakfa is pegged at 15 to the US dollar, a rate the report calls severely overvalued, and cash access is restricted. [25] The Bisha copper mine, a venture of China's Zijin Mining and the state firm ENAMCO, was historically the only stable source of foreign income, and the report says mining revenue is not accounted for or used for public needs. China is the only active foreign investor in mining. [25]

Borders with Ethiopia have been closed since 2019, and Eritrea is the only African country outside the African Continental Free Trade Area. Most Eritreans depend on diaspora remittances, and a 2 percent diaspora tax is often collected under coercion. [25] The UN Special Rapporteur says authorities impose the same 2 percent tax and require letters of regret for consular services. [9]

lenses.international: Al Jazeera reports that Yemane said the US sanctions caused major damage to the country. [3]
lenses.scholar: The Bertelsmann index scores Eritrea 1 out of 10 on market organisation, monetary stability, fiscal stability and private enterprise. [25]

sections.title: National service without end, a 2 percent tax on exiles and the last-ranked press in the world
sections.body_md:
RSF ranks Eritrea 180th of 180 countries in its 2026 index, with a score of 10.24, and lists 10 journalists and 4 media workers as currently detained. It says Dawit Isaak, a Swedish-Eritrean journalist, has been held incommunicado since 2001. [26] HRW says the fate of 10 independent journalists arrested since September 2001, and of 11 former officials known as the G-15, remains unknown. It adds that the legislature has not met since 2010. [4]

National service should legally last 18 months but has been extended indefinitely, and conscientious objection is prohibited. [4] The UN Special Rapporteur, Mohamed Abdelsalam Babiker, reports round-ups and forced conscription in the Segheneyti subregion between July and December 2025, including house sealings and the re-recruitment of older people. He finds that disappearances and arbitrary detention may amount to crimes against humanity. [9] The UN estimates that more than 10,000 people are held arbitrarily, according to HRW. [27]

The Human Rights Council renewed the rapporteur's mandate on 6 July 2026 by 23 votes to 6, with 17 abstentions. Eritrea's ambassador had said Eritrea would stop engaging with the mandate if it was renewed. [28] Eritrea remains one of very few countries never to have accepted a visit from a UN independent human rights expert. [4]

lenses.international: HRW and RSF report the detention of journalists, religious detainees and draft evaders, and the ban on independent media. [4][26]
lenses.scholar: The Bertelsmann index scores Eritrea 1 out of 10 on free and fair elections, freedom of expression and the independence of the judiciary, and says the 1997 constitution remains unimplemented. [25]

sections.title: More than 679,000 Eritreans are abroad, and the countries that took them in are closing doors
sections.body_md:
UNHCR knew of more than 679,000 Eritrean refugees and asylum seekers by December 2025, with Ethiopia, Sudan, Germany, Uganda, Egypt and Switzerland hosting the most. Its 2026 guidance note urges states to admit Eritreans, respect non-refoulement and consider a prima facie approach where large numbers arrive with similar claims. [29] The UN Special Rapporteur documents deportations, registration suspensions in Kenya and Ethiopia, and extortion and detention in Egypt. [9]

The Mixed Migration Centre's report finds that Eritreans' access to documents, registration and livelihoods has shrunk, that camps in Ethiopia and Sudan have high protection needs, and that Cairo, Kampala and Addis Ababa are becoming the main places where Eritreans find some safety, with rising risk of detention and deportation. It counts about 80,000 self-reported Eritreans in Addis Ababa and about 60,000 in the Barahle and Aysaita camps in Afar. It says sea arrivals in Europe fell almost 90 percent between the mid-2010s and 2024, and expects the drop may not last. [30]

HRW reports that Ethiopian police shot and killed several Eritreans in Addis Ababa in 2025 while they fled arrest, and that Switzerland decided in February 2025 to end development aid by May because Eritrea refused to accept deportees. [4]

lenses.international: HRW and UNHCR report shrinking protection for Eritreans in Ethiopia, Sudan, Egypt and elsewhere. [4][29]
lenses.scholar: The Mixed Migration Centre finds that shifting regional alliances have made asylum harder to reach and raised the risk of deportation to Eritrea. [30]

timeline.text: Eritrea becomes independent from Ethiopia; no national election has been held since.
A border war with Ethiopia begins and runs to 2000.
Independent media are banned and 10 journalists are arrested.
Eritrea and Ethiopia make peace after Abiy Ahmed takes power.
Eritrean forces fight alongside Ethiopia against the TPLF in the Tigray war.
The Pretoria agreement ends the Tigray war; Eritrea is not a party.
Abiy makes remarks on sea access that Eritrea later calls a declaration of war.
The UN Human Rights Council renews the Eritrea rapporteur's mandate over Eritrea's objection.
Eritrea announces its withdrawal from IGAD.
Crisis Group publishes its briefing naming Assab as the likeliest target of a limited Ethiopian campaign.
The Human Rights Council renews the rapporteur's mandate by 23 votes to 6.
Egypt, Eritrea and Somalia meet in Cairo with a US envoy, according to The Reporter.
US sanctions on Eritrea's ruling party and military lapse.
Fighting resumes in Tigray between Ethiopian forces and a TPLF-led alliance of seven groups.
Ethiopia expels 10 Eritrean diplomats and Eritrea severs diplomatic ties.
Ethiopia writes to the UN Security Council accusing Eritrea of an all-out invasion.
Rubio calls Abiy and urges de-escalation.
Clashes around Rama near the Eritrean border begin; fighting at Badme follows from 9 November.
Critical Threats reports unconfirmed Eritrean mobilisation at Sawa and a UN delegation visit to Mekelle.

scores.coverage_basis: AFP, Reuters and AP file on Eritrea mainly when the Ethiopia dispute flares, and no foreign correspondent can report freely from inside the country [2][7]. HRW, Crisis Group, Critical Threats and the UN Rapporteur publish steadily, but domestic reporting does not exist because independent media are banned [4][8][13].

severity.basis: Ethiopia and Eritrea accuse each other of aggression, ties are cut, and trackers report fighting near Rama and Badme in November, though troop claims are unverified [13][2][7].
More than 679,000 Eritreans are refugees or asylum seekers abroad, humanitarian access is restricted and Eritrea ranks 178 of 193 on the Human Development Index [29][9].

RSF ranks the press last of 180, national service is indefinite, no election has been held since 1993 and the UN Special Rapporteur finds detention practices may amount to crimes against humanity [26][4][9].
No state budget has been published since independence, debt was 164 percent of GDP in 2022 and the nakfa is pegged at a severely overvalued rate [25].
Diplomatic ties were cut on 1 October, a mobilisation at Sawa was reported on 14 November and the UN Rapporteur reports renewed round-ups for conscription [1][13][9].

parts.basis: The US let sanctions lapse citing regional interests, Egypt and Eritrea issued a joint Red Sea declaration, and Rubio and Massad Boulos are engaged on the dispute [3][21][13].
Eritrea's own economy is small and opaque, but Assab sits on the Red Sea and Horn Review says the Djibouti corridor carries over 90 percent of Ethiopia's trade [25][19].
Ethiopia accuses Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt of backing the Tigray alliance, and analysts warn of wider effects on Sudan, Somalia and Red Sea security [12][10].
More than 679,000 Eritreans live abroad, and the UN Rapporteur documents diaspora taxation and intimidation in host countries including Germany [29][9].
Ethiopia invokes Article 51, Eritrea invokes Chapter VII, and the UN Secretary-General's office urges both to honour the Algiers Agreement [7][6][23].

summary: Eritrea matters beyond its borders because a war with Ethiopia would pull in Sudan, Egypt and Red Sea shipping, and because its exiles number more than 679,000, rather than through trade or its own economy [10][29].
gi.up: Direct, confirmed fighting between the Eritrean and Ethiopian armies, or an Ethiopian move on Assab.
gi.down: A return to diplomatic channels between Asmara and Addis Ababa and a verified withdrawal from the border areas.

gaps: Eritrea has no independent domestic press (RSF ranks it last of 180), so the local lens rests on Ethiopian and Kenyan outlets (The Reporter, the Nation, Horn Review, Garowe Online) and not on reporting from inside the country.
State sources such as Shabait and the Ministry of Information website were not opened. Asmara's positions come from wire and regional reports of Yemane Gebremeskel's statements and posts on X.
Diaspora outlets (Radio Erena in Paris, Awate, Eritrea Hub, Tesfanews) were not read for current news; the only item on Radio Erena is an RSF description from 2016.

Troop movements, the 60 km advance, Eritrean casualties and the Sawa mobilisation are unverified. Reuters, AP and Critical Threats describe Asmara's response differently (did not deny, neither confirmed nor denied, denied).

Source conflicts: the sanctions lapse is dated 18 September by Horn Review and 19 September by Al Jazeera (a Saturday); Ethiopia's letter is dated Thursday by AFP and Friday by AP; the first IGAD exit is 2003 or 2007; the legislature last met in 2010 (HRW) or 2001 to 2002 (BTI); the Tigray war toll is 100,000 or more (Semafor) or 600,000 (Al Jazeera).

No current GDP, inflation or budget figure was found. BTI says the World Bank and IMF have not published them; the IMF, World Bank and AfDB primary pages were not opened and an automated Rio Times article on the economy was set aside.
No OCHA, WFP or IPC data on hunger inside Eritrea were found, and the stunting figure in BTI (about 50 percent, citing UNICEF 2023) was not checked at source.

Horn Review pieces are from an Addis Ababa outlet, are partly opinion and rely on anonymous sources; they are used with attribution only. The UN Special Rapporteur report, UNHCR guidance note, BTI and Crisis Group briefing were read through summaries, not in full.
Religious detainee numbers and the G-15 and journalist cases rest on HRW and the UN Rapporteur alone. Nothing after 17 November was found.

Reporters: no Eritrea-based reporter can be named, so the list holds Ethiopian reporters, an exile broadcaster, researchers and a UN expert. Books: the newest verified title is from 2019. Podcast and media items predate the current crisis (2021).

reporters.name: Martin Plaut
reporters.role: Journalist and author; Senior Researcher, Institute of Commonwealth Studies and King's College London
reporters.bio: Hurst describes him as a former Africa Editor of the BBC World Service and the author of Understanding Eritrea. He also wrote the 3 May 2026 blog summary of UNHCR's Eritrea guidance note.
reporters.why: His writing tracks Eritrean human rights and refugee policy closely and is one of the main English-language sources on the country.

reporters.name: Meron Estefanos
reporters.bio: RSF's 2016 profile of Radio Erena says her programmes speak with Eritreans held by traffickers in the Sinai and work to secure their release.

reporters.bio: Author of the 17 November 2026 Ethiopia War Security Review, with contributor Alexander Brown.

local_md:
The Nation reports Ethiopian army forces had reached Zalambessa, on the Ethiopian side of the border, according to six sources, and that it was unclear whether Eritrean troops or rebels remained there. [6]

The Nation noted that the Zalambessa picture was unclear in mid-October, with a pro-government militia spokesman not confirming that the army controlled the town. [6]

The Reporter in Addis Ababa carried Abiy's parliamentary line and Asmara's reply side by side. [5]

The Reporter carried Boulos's August denial of an anti-Ethiopia bloc. No Eritrea-based outlet reported on the lapse in anything this draft could read. [21]

Ethiopian outlets, The Reporter and Horn Review among them, frame Egypt and Eritrea as aligned against Ethiopia, and the Reporter's own account of the Cairo meeting is presented as reported. [21][24]
international_md:
AFP, AP and Reuters carry both governments' claims. Reuters witnesses saw dozens of Eritrean soldiers in Adigrat, and none of the wires could verify the 60 km advance. [12][2][7]

AFP, Anadolu and AP report the same incidents and flag each casualty and territorial claim as unverified. [17][14]

AFP carries Yemane's Golan precedent claim and his charge that Ethiopia has been at war with Eritrea since 2023. [11]

AFP, AP and Reuters report the lapse, and Semafor reports that no official reason was given. [3][20]

Africanews and Yahoo carry Eritrea's exit from IGAD and the UN's call to recommit to the Algiers Agreement. [22][23]

Al Jazeera reports that Yemane said the US sanctions caused major damage to the country. [3]

HRW and RSF report the detention of journalists, religious detainees and draft evaders, and the ban on independent media. [4][26]

HRW and UNHCR report shrinking protection for Eritreans in Ethiopia, Sudan, Egypt and elsewhere. [4][29]
scholar_md:
Hossamaldeen Ibrahim of the Bloomsbury Intelligence and Security Institute says severed ties removed the main crisis-management channel, and Matthias Rompel of Giessen University says Eritrean involvement is hard to verify independently. [10]

Critical Threats and ACLED are the main trackers, and Critical Threats marks each claim it could not confirm. [13]

Crisis Group and Chatham House both treat Assab as the focal point and urge preventive diplomacy and pressure on Ethiopia not to move on it. [8][18]

Horn Review notes the lapse in its October brief on Ethiopia's northern crisis and dates it to 18 September. [19]

Horn Review's analysis of Egypt, Eritrea and eastern Sudan is an opinion piece and rests on second-hand claims. [24]

The Bertelsmann index scores Eritrea 1 out of 10 on market organisation, monetary stability, fiscal stability and private enterprise. [25]

The Bertelsmann index scores Eritrea 1 out of 10 on free and fair elections, freedom of expression and the independence of the judiciary, and says the 1997 constitution remains unimplemented. [25]

The Mixed Migration Centre finds that shifting regional alliances have made asylum harder to reach and raised the risk of deportation to Eritrea. [30]
